title: Substantial evidence, contrary evidence, and standards of review
shortTitle: Substantial evidence, contrary evidence, and standards of review
summary: Substantial evidence is relevant evidence a reasonable mind could accept as adequate, assessed with the entire record and the governing statute.
notes:
Section 706(2)(E) expressly applies to formal proceedings and other statutorily specified on-the-record hearings; organic statutes may also prescribe substantial-evidence review. Universal Camera requires attention to contrary evidence and examiner findings, while preserving the agency’s authority to choose between fairly conflicting accounts.

The notes illustrate different problems. Allentown Mack upheld the Board’s reasonable-doubt policy but rejected its evidentiary application after important contrary evidence was disregarded. Biestek rejected a categorical rule that a vocational expert’s refusal to disclose supporting data always prevents the testimony from being substantial evidence; reliability remains contextual. Dickinson v. Zurko required the APA approach to agency review rather than importing court-to-court clearly-erroneous review based on an uncertain historical exception. The verbal distinction can be subtle without becoming meaningless.

ADAPSO’s D.C. Circuit approach equates the required quantum of factual support under substantial evidence and arbitrary-and-capricious review, while locating that support in different kinds of administrative records. Safe Extensions applied that reasoning to an informal FAA decision treating competing runway-light products differently without supporting evidence. The notes also identify organic-statute decisions that distinguish the standards. The conceptual problem asks whether later judicial convergence can be reconciled with the understanding of the APA’s drafters; it does not assume that historical meaning has already settled the answer.
